policy_title: Introduce a New Industrial Strategy and National Wealth Fund
stated: Labour will introduce a new, mission-driven industrial strategy focused on future-oriented sectors like financial services, advanced manufacturing, and creative industries, supported by a statutory Industrial Strategy Council for expert advice. They will establish a National Wealth Fund, capitalised with £7.3 billion, to make transformative public investments (e.g., in gigafactories, steel, carbon capture, hydrogen, ports) to attract private investment and create jobs across the country.

source.quote:
Labour will introduce a new industrial strategy. Our approach will be mission-driven and focused on the future. We will work in partnership with industry to seize opportunities and remove barriers to growth. Critically, we will end short-term economic policy making with the establishment of an Industrial Strategy Council, on a statutory footing, to provide expert advice. Financial services are one of Britain’s greatest success stories. Labour will create the conditions to support innovation and growth in the sector, through supporting new technology, including Open Banking and Open Finance and ensuring a pro-innovation regulatory framework. To realise these opportunities Labour will establish a National Wealth Fund. Capitalised with £7.3 billion over the course of the next Parliament, the National Wealth Fund will have a remit to support Labour’s growth and clean energy missions, making transformative investments across every part of the country. The fund will have a target of attracting three pounds of private investment for every one pound of public investment, creating jobs across the country. We plan to allocate: 
• £1.8 billion to upgrade ports and build supply chains across the UK 
• £1.5 billion to new gigafactories so our automotive industry leads the world 
• £2.5 billion to rebuild our steel industry 
• £1 billion to accelerate the deployment of carbon capture 
• £500 million to support the manufacturing of green hydrogen.

bearing_set.reason: The policy explicitly targets job creation across the country through sectoral investments (gigafactories, steel, advanced manufacturing) and a mission-driven industrial strategy — directly bearing on employment rates, job quality, and regional economic security.

The National Wealth Fund explicitly commits capital to carbon capture, hydrogen, and gigafactories, all of which are direct levers on the UK's emissions trajectory and clean-energy infrastructure — earning a real verdict on emissions and environmental quality.

An explicit mission-driven industrial strategy targeting productivity, business investment, and economic opportunity in future-oriented sectors is a direct lever on aggregate prosperity and living standards, with a dual near-term (public capital deployment) and long-term (productivity uplift, crowded-in private investment) horizon.

A £7.3 billion public capitalisation commitment materially affects the public balance sheet; the contested question of whether this constitutes productive investment (improving long-run sustainability) or adds to the borrowing burden (worsening it) is a real fiscal sustainability debate with a concrete mechanism.

membership_note: Four fundamentals: the policy's primary purpose lands on O13 (aggregate prosperity/investment), with a non-negligible O4 jobs/quality-of-work effect, a genuine O6 clean-energy channel via the specific NWF investment targets, and a material O12 fiscal-sustainability question around the £7.3bn capitalisation. Regional inequality (O14) was considered but the mechanism from sectoral investment to Gini narrowing is too indirect to clear the non-negligible bar at this stage.
